Then the places where numbers, figures and references enter the text. And last a render from a clean session, which is the test that a report makes everything that it uses. ::: # Source and output {#source-and-output .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Section 1 ::: ::: notes Section one is about the difference between a source and its output. A Quarto document is plain text, and we start with why that matters. Then the three kinds of content that the file holds, and the two programs that turn it into a report when you render it. Then we open the report of the workspace in Positron, run its chunks one at a time in the console, and preview the whole report, which is the first task of your own. ::: ## Plain-text file formats {#plain-text-is-the-format-that-survives} ::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
.RCode only, with prose in comments.
.mdProse only: headings, lists, links, and no code.
.RmdProse and R, rendered together. R only.
.qmdProse and R, Python or Julia. The format of the course.
::: ::: {.fragment .small .fs-80} Every one of these is a **plain text file**. You can open it in anything, compare two versions of it line by line, email it, and read it in twenty years. A `.docx` with pasted output is not plain text, and nothing in it records which numbers came from which code. ::: ::: notes Four file types, in increasing order of what they hold. A dot R file is code with comments. A Markdown file is prose with no code. An R Markdown file is prose and R together, rendered into one document. And a Quarto file is the same idea, except that the code can be R or Python or Julia. What they have in common is that every one of them is a plain text file. You can open it in any editor, see exactly what changed between two versions, email it, and still read it in twenty years. Compare that with a Word document holding numbers that you pasted in from somewhere. It looks the same on the page, but nothing in it records which number came from which line of code, which is how the old value of a number that you have since recomputed can still be sitting in the paper. ::: ## What a .qmd file holds {#what-a-qmd-file-holds .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="57%"} ::: {.fs-110} ````markdown --- title: "A first report" format: html --- ## What the data hold The housing-audit data hold one row per email. ```{{r}} audit <- readr::read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv") nrow(audit) ``` ```` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="43%"} ::: {.small} - **The YAML header**, between two lines of three hyphens: the title and the settings that decide what comes out - **The prose**, in Markdown: `##` opens a heading, `**text**` sets text in bold - **The code chunks**, opened by three backticks and `{r}`: run while the document is built, with each result placed where its chunk stands ::: ::: :::: ::: notes A dot qmd file is plain text, which any editor can open, and it holds three kinds of content. The header comes first, fenced above and below by a line of three hyphens. It is written in YAML and holds the metadata of the document, such as the title, together with the settings that decide what kind of document comes out. The prose is Markdown, a light convention in which two hashes open a heading and two asterisks on each side set a word in bold. And the code chunks are blocks of R, each opened by three backticks and the name of the engine in braces. The chunks run while the document is built, and the result of each is placed in the finished document at the point where its chunk stands. This file is complete: render it, and it gives a page with a heading, a sentence and the number of emails. ::: ## What happens when you render {#how-a-document-becomes-a-document} ![](pics/tools/render-pipeline.png){fig-align="center" width="62%" fig-alt="A diagram of rendering: a qmd file goes to knitr, which writes a md file, which pandoc turns into a Word document, a PDF or a web page."} ::: {.small .fs-80} You write **one** source file. Rendering runs its code, puts the results in place, and produces whatever output you asked for from that one source. An error in a chunk stops the render, and Quarto names the chunk at which it stopped. ::: ::: notes And this is what happens when you render. You write one source file, with prose and code together. Knitr, or Jupyter if you are working in Python, hands every chunk to R in a fresh session, collects whatever comes back, and writes a plain Markdown file with the results pasted in after the code that produced them. Pandoc, a document converter, then turns that file into whatever you asked for: a Word document for your co-author, a PDF for the journal, a web page for your project, slides like these. So there is one place where a number is computed, and every output shows the same number. Because the code runs before any typesetting, an error in a chunk halts the render, and no new output appears at all. Quarto names the chunk that failed, which is the first reason to give every chunk a label. ::: ## The report of the workspace {#the-report-of-the-workspace .smaller} ::: {.small} - `index.qmd` is the report: the five tasks of the exercise of the case and the preregistration block, with the reasoning written around the code and each result printed beside the sentences that discuss it - `working_script.R` holds the same analysis as a plain script, which is quicker to experiment with - A render writes the report to `_site/index.html`, because the workspace is a Quarto project whose output goes to `_site` ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Never edit the rendered output. Every render writes it afresh from the source, and the `.qmd` is the file that you keep, version and share. ::: ::: notes Your workspace holds the same analysis twice. The working script takes the tasks as a plain R script that you step through in the console, as we did in the last session. index dot qmd is the same work as a report, with the reasoning written around the code and the results printed beside the sentences that discuss them. The script is quicker to experiment with. The report is the thing that you can hand to somebody, and its results cannot go stale, because they are computed again from the data every time that the file is rendered. The workspace is a Quarto project whose output goes to a folder called underscore site, so the report becomes underscore site slash index dot html. [advance] That file is disposable, since every render writes it afresh, so never edit it: the source is what you keep. ::: ## Chunks in the console {#chunks-in-the-console .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.fs-110} ```{{r}} #| label: count-emails # How many emails, and what came back? audit |> datawizard::data_summary(emails = n(), bounced = sum(is.na(reply)), delivered = sum(!is.na(reply)), replies = sum(reply %in% 1), coded = sum(!is.na(named))) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` emails | bounced | delivered | replies | coded ---------------------------------------------- 1014 | 23 | 991 | 563 | 558 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.small} - **Run Cell**, **Run Next Cell** and **Run Above** stand over every chunk - Ctrl+Shift+Enter runs the chunk under the cursor, and Ctrl+Enter one statement inside it - The objects in the console exist only in your session: a render starts a fresh R process and never uses them ::: ::: :::: ::: notes While you write a report, you rarely render it after every change. You run its chunks one at a time instead, in the console, where each result appears at once and the objects that a chunk makes stay in the session for the next chunk. Over every chunk stand three links: Run Cell, Run Next Cell, and Run Above, which runs every chunk above, the quick way back to the state of the report at a given point after a restart. Control, Shift and Enter runs the chunk under the cursor, and Control and Enter a single statement inside it, as in a script. This is the first chunk of Task 2, and it prints the counts that you met in the last two sessions. But the objects in the console exist only in your session. A render starts a fresh R process, runs every chunk from the top and discards the process at the end. ::: ## The preview {#the-preview .smaller} ::: {.small} - **Preview** (Ctrl+Shift+K) renders the report and shows it in the Viewer, beside the source - A terminal called Quarto Preview lists the chunks as they run, and ends with `Output created: _site\index.html` and `Watching files for changes` - Saving alone leaves the preview as it was: press Ctrl+Shift+K again, or tick **Render on Save** - RStudio: the **Render** button. VS Code: **Quarto: Preview**, with Quarto installed ::: ::: notes Two commands turn the report into a document. Preview, the button at the top of the editor or Control, Shift and K, renders the report and shows the result in the Viewer on the right of the window, where you can read it beside the source. Positron opens a terminal called Quarto Preview under the editor and runs Quarto there, and the terminal lists the chunks as knitr runs them, which takes a little while, because the report fits several models. It ends with the name of the file that it wrote and the line Watching files for changes. When you change the report, saving alone leaves the preview as it was, so press Control, Shift and K again, or tick Render on Save, which renders the report every time that you save. In RStudio the same button is called Render. ::: ## Hands-on 1 – Chunks and a preview {#hands-on-1-chunks-and-a-preview .smaller} ::: {.small} 1. Open `index.qmd`, click into the setup chunk at the top, and press Ctrl+Shift+Enter 2. Run the chunks of Task 2 one at a time, from `count-emails` to `fig-names`, with Run Cell or Shift+Enter 3. Read the figure: which name received the fewest greetings by name? Note it in the report as a comment, as its TODO asks 4. Preview the report with Ctrl+Shift+K, and find the box of Task 2 in the Viewer ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Santiago, with 37.1% of the replies to emails signed with that name greeting the sender by name. ::: ::: notes Your turn. Open the report, click into the setup chunk at the top and run it with Control, Shift and Enter: it reads the housing-audit data and loads the helpers, and the Variables pane lists what it made. Then run the chunks of Task 2, one at a time, from the counts to the figure of the six names, which appears in the Plots pane. The figure answers the question of the TODO in Task 2, which name received the fewest greetings by name, and the answer goes into the report as a comment in the chunk. Then preview the whole report and find the box of Task 2, where the same counts and the same figure now stand in the document. If you work in RStudio, the green arrow on each chunk runs it, and Render previews the report. Take the time you need. ::: # The header and the chunks {#the-header-and-the-chunks .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Section 2 ::: ::: notes Section two reads the two parts of the report that tell Quarto what to do. The header at the top sets the title, the date and the format of the whole document, and it is written in YAML, which is fussy in a few ways that are worth learning before they bite. Then the chunks of code, and the options on their first lines that decide what a chunk shows: its code, its results, both or neither, and what happens when it fails. The task at the end changes an option and breaks the header on purpose. ::: ## The YAML header {#the-yaml-header .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="66%"} ::: {.fs-100} ```{.yaml code-line-numbers="false"} --- title: "Testing the robustness of a published claim: the housing-audit case" author: "Pair: [names]" date: today format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 2 code-fold: false df-print: paged execute: message: false warning: false knitr: opts_chunk: fig-width: 8 fig-height: 5 --- ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="34%"} ::: {.small .fs-85} - `date: today` fills in the date of the render - `format:` decides what comes out: a web page with a table of contents, code shown open, and data frames as paged tables - `execute:` sets options for every chunk at once - `knitr:` passes options to knitr, here the size of every figure ::: ::: :::: ::: notes The header of the report uses most of the keys that ordinary work needs. Title and author print at the top of the document. date colon today is a keyword of Quarto that fills in the date at render time, so a report rendered next month carries the date of next month without anybody remembering to change it. Everything under format configures the web page: a table of contents built from the first two levels of headings, the code shown open, and data frames printed as small paged tables. The execute block sets options for every chunk at once, here hiding the start-up messages of packages and the warnings that would clutter a report meant for a reader. And the knitr block fixes the size of every figure unless a chunk asks for another. Adding pdf or docx under format would give those formats as well, from the same file. ::: ## The rules of YAML {#the-rules-of-yaml .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.small} - Indent with spaces, never tabs: two for each level - `key: value`, with a space after the colon - A string that holds a colon goes in quotes, as the title does - `true` and `false` in lower case ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Without the space in `toc: true`, the render stops before any chunk runs. The caret sits under line 8, but the mistake is on line 7, so read the line above it as well. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} ![](../tools/images/quarto/task-yaml-error.png){fig-alt="The Quarto Preview terminal reporting ERROR: YAMLException: bad indentation of a mapping entry (8:14), with lines 5 to 10 of the header, toc:true on line 7, a caret under line 8, and the start of a stack trace." width="100%" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: :::: ::: notes YAML is fussy in a small number of ways, and a malformed header is probably the most common reason why a document that rendered yesterday will not render today. Indentation is by spaces, never tabs, and two spaces for each level is the convention. Every entry is a key, a colon, a space and a value. A string that contains a colon has to be quoted, which is why the title of the report sits inside quotation marks. And true and false are written in lower case. [advance] This is what a broken header looks like: the space after the colon in toc true was deleted, and the render stops before any chunk runs. YAML reads toc colon true as one plain word and notices that something is wrong only on the next line, which is why the caret points one line too low. ::: ## Chunks and their options {#chunks-and-their-options .smaller} ::: {.fs-110} ```{{r}} #| label: setup #| include: false audit <- readr::read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) source("R/spec_tools.R") ``` ::: ::: {.fs-65} | Option | What it does | |---|---| | `label` | Names the chunk; Quarto prints the label when the chunk fails | | `echo: false` | The code runs and its results appear; the code is hidden | | `output: false` | The code runs and is shown; its results are hidden | | `include: false` | The code runs; neither the code nor its results appear | | `eval: false` | The code is shown and not run | | `error: true` | An error is printed in the document instead of stopping the render | | `message: false`, `warning: false` | The messages and warnings of R are hidden | ::: ::: notes A chunk opens with three backticks and the name of the engine in braces, and its options follow as comment lines that begin with a hash and a vertical bar. The option lines are YAML again, so the same rules about colons and spaces apply. On the slide is the setup chunk of the report, without its comments, which reads the data and loads the helpers. Seven options cover almost everything that the report needs. The label names the chunk, and Quarto prints it when the chunk fails. echo, output and include are the three that are most easily confused: echo governs the code, output governs the results, and include turns both off while still running the chunk. The setup chunk of the report is marked include false, because it has to run first and no reader needs to see it. Of the seven, output is the only one that Quarto adds to the options of knitr. ::: ## Two options in the report {#two-options-in-the-report .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.fs-110} ```{{r}} #| label: submit-exploration #| eval: false submit_exploration() ``` ::: ::: {.small} `eval: false`: the reader sees what to run, and rendering the report never sends a submission to the class chart. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.fs-110} ```{{r}} #| label: try-off-curve #| error: true try_spec(model = "three_group") ``` ::: ::: {.small} `error: true`: the helper refuses the option and gives its reason, the message is printed in the report, and the render carries on. ::: ::: :::: ::: notes Two chunks of the report show what the options are for. The first is the step that sends your exploratory result to the class chart on the second day. It is marked eval false, so the reader sees what to run, and rendering the report never sends a submission. The second does the opposite job. In Task 4 the report deliberately asks for an option of the menu that is not on the curve, so that you can read the reason why the helper refuses it. Without error true, the refusal would stop the render. With it, the message is printed in the report and the render carries on to the next chunk. In every other chunk an error should stop the render, because a report that carries on past a broken chunk prints results that nobody checked. ::: ## Where options are set {#where-options-are-set .smaller .deepdive run="quarto"} ::: {.small} 1. **On the chunk**, in its `#|` lines 2. **In the header** of the document, under `execute:` 3. **In `_metadata.yml`**, for every document of a folder 4. **In `_quarto.yml`**, for the whole project ::: ::: {.fragment .small} The setting nearest to the chunk wins. The report hides messages and warnings in its header, the project file of the workspace sets `freeze: auto`, and the slides of this course share their theme and their bibliography through the `_metadata.yml` of their folder. ::: ::: notes The same options can be written at four levels: on a chunk, in the header of a document under execute, in a file called underscore metadata dot yml that governs every document of a folder, and in the configuration of the whole project. Where an option is set at more than one level, the setting nearest to the chunk wins, so an option on a chunk beats the header, which beats the file of the folder, which beats the configuration of the project. The report suppresses messages and warnings for the whole document in its header, and the project file of the workspace sets freeze auto for every document, which the last section comes back to. These slides are built the same way: the theme, the bibliography and the options shared by every deck are written once, in the metadata file of the folder that holds the decks. ::: ## Hands-on 2 – Options and the header {#hands-on-2-options-and-the-header .smaller} ::: {.small} 1. In the chunk `count-emails`, click at the end of `#| label: count-emails`, press Enter, and type `echo: false`. Save, and preview with Ctrl+Shift+K: the counts appear without their code 2. Replace `echo: false` with `eval: false`, and preview again: the code is back and the counts are gone. Then delete the line 3. In the header, delete the space in `toc: true`, save, and preview. Read the message, restore the space, and start the preview again ::: ::: notes Your turn, with two small edits and one deliberate mistake. In the chunk that counts the emails, add an option line under the label. Positron starts the new line with the hash and the bar for you, so type echo colon false, save and preview: in the Viewer, the box of Task 2 shows the table of counts with no code above it. Then change echo to eval and preview again, and the code comes back while the counts disappear, because the chunk no longer runs. Delete the line so that the chunk is as it was. Then break the header: delete the space after the colon in toc true, save and preview, and read the message from the top. A broken header also stops the preview itself, so restore the space and press Control, Shift and K to start it again. Take the time you need. ::: # Numbers, figures and references {#numbers-figures-and-references .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Section 3 ::: ::: notes Section three is about the places where results enter the text. A number typed into a sentence is a copy, which goes stale as soon as the data or the code change, and inline code computes it at every render instead. Figures and tables get a caption and a number, and the prose can refer to them by that number. And citations come from a bibliography file, so that the list of references is built from what the text actually cites. The task at the end puts a computed number and a reference to a figure into the report. ::: ## Inline code {#inline-code .smaller} ::: {.small} Under the chunk of 8PTRZ, one of the five analysts whose reanalyses Task 3 reproduces, the report gives the value of the test as typed text: ::: ::: {.fs-110} ```markdown The test gives **X-squared = 14.265** on 1 df, the value on record for 8PTRZ. ``` ::: ::: {.small} Inline code computes it from the table made by the chunk above it, at every render: ::: ::: {.fs-110} ```markdown The test gives X-squared = `r round(chisq.test(tab_8ptrz)$statistic, 3)` on 1 df, the value on record for 8PTRZ. ``` ::: ::: {.fragment .small} which renders as "The test gives X-squared = 14.265 on 1 df, the value on record for 8PTRZ." Change a filter, render again, and the sentence follows. ::: ::: notes Here is the habit that separates a report from a document with numbers pasted into it. A number typed into a sentence is a copy, and copies go stale: you change a filter, rerun the analysis, and the old number sits on in paragraph three. Inline code fixes that. Between single backticks, the letter r and a piece of code: when the report renders, the code runs, and its value takes its place in the sentence. Task 3 of the report reproduces the chi-square test of 8PTRZ, one of the five analysts, and the sentence under the chunk gives the value as typed text. The inline expression computes it instead, from the table that the chunk above it made. [advance] The rendered sentence reads exactly as before, but now its number comes from the same run as the tables and the figures, so the three cannot disagree. ::: ## Captions and cross-references {#captions-and-cross-references .smaller} ::: {.fs-100} ```{{r}} #| label: fig-names #| fig-cap: "Replies that greeted the sender by name, by the name that signed the email." #| fig-height: 3.6 # The share greeted by name for each of the six names, from the lowest greeted <- audit |> datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |> datawizard::data_summary(greeted_pct = 100 * mean(named), by = c("group", "name")) ``` ::: ::: {.small} - A label that begins `fig-` and a `fig-cap` make a numbered figure, and `tbl-` with a `tbl-cap` a numbered table - `(@fig-names)` after "a gap of about 20 points" renders as "(Figure 1)", a link to the figure - A reference that Quarto cannot resolve prints as `?@fig-names` ::: ::: notes A figure drawn by a chunk becomes a numbered, captioned figure that the prose can refer to once two conditions are met: the chunk has a caption, and its label begins with fig dash. The report draws its figure of the six names that way, and the slide shows the opening lines of that chunk, which go on to order the names and draw the bars. With the prefix in place, Quarto numbers the figure, and writing at fig dash names in a sentence gives "Figure 1" in the rendered text, as a link that takes the reader to the figure. Tables work in the same way, with tbl dash and a table caption. The report already has three labelled figures, and nothing in it refers to them yet, so adding a reference is a one-word edit. If the label loses its prefix, the reference prints with a question mark, which is how Quarto reports a reference that it cannot resolve. ::: ## Citations {#citations .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="48%"} ::: {.fs-100} ```bibtex @article{EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, author = {Einstein, Katherine Levine and Glick, David M.}, year = 2017, journal = {American Journal of Political Science}, doi = {10.1111/ajps.12252} } ``` ::: ::: {.small} A record of `references.bib`, shortened. The word after the opening brace is the **citekey**, and `bibliography: references.bib` in the header points at the file. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="52%"} ::: {.fs-65} | You write | It renders as | |---|---| | `[@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]` | [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect] | | `@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect` | @EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect | | `[@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, p. 100]` | [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, p. 100] | ::: ::: {.small} The list of references is built from what the text cites, at the place of `::: {#refs}`. The right-hand column of the table cites the paper of the original authors (OAs), and the last slide of this deck lists it. ::: ::: :::: ::: notes Add a bibliography key to the header, pointing at a BibTeX file, and citations start working. A BibTeX file is a plain-text database with one record for each work, and this is the record of the paper behind the housing-audit case, shortened to the fields that a citation needs. The word just after the opening brace is the citekey, the name by which you cite the work. Almost nobody types these records by hand: a reference manager such as Zotero holds the library and exports the file. Square brackets around an at sign and the key give a citation in brackets, the key alone gives one in the text, and a page goes after a comma. The list of references is assembled from what you actually cite. The report of the workspace lists its five references by hand, and turning that list into a bibliography file is a good exercise for after the course. ::: ## Hands-on 3 – A number and Figure 1 {#hands-on-3-a-number-and-figure-1 .smaller} ::: {.small} 1. In the box of Task 3, find the section of the analyst whose analysis you would reproduce, and the sentence under its chunk that gives the value as typed text 2. Replace the typed value with inline code computed from the object made by the chunk, save, and preview: the sentence reads as before 3. Under the figure of Task 2, add `(@fig-names)` after "a gap of about 20 points", save, and preview: "(Figure 1)" 4. Change the label of the chunk to `names-figure`, preview, read `?@fig-names`, and change it back ::: ::: {.fragment .small} For 8PTRZ the expression is `round(chisq.test(tab_8ptrz)$statistic, 3)`; for 25N5D, `round(prop.test(counts_25n5d$greetings, counts_25n5d$emails)$statistic, 3)`. ::: ::: notes Your turn, with the two edits that make a report trustworthy. In the box of Task 3, choose the analyst whose analysis you would most like to reproduce, and find the sentence under its chunk, which gives the value of the test as typed text. Replace the typed value with inline code that computes it from the object that the chunk makes, then save and preview: the sentence reads as it did before, but the source now tells you where the number comes from. Then the reference. Under the figure of Task 2, add the reference to the figure after the words "a gap of about 20 points", and preview: the sentence now carries a link to Figure 1. Finally, break the label on purpose, read what Quarto prints, and put the label back. [advance] Two of the expressions are on the slide. Take the time you need. ::: # A clean render {#a-clean-render .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Section 4 ::: ::: notes Section four is about the render itself. A render can fail, and the message that it prints says where and why, if you read it from the top. Then the habit that the whole day leads up to: a render from a clean session, which shows whether the report makes everything that it uses or leans on an object that only your console holds. We end with the steps that lead from a folder that renders to a public record, and with a last task. ::: ## A failed render {#a-failed-render .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="65%"} ![](../tools/images/quarto/positron-render-error.png){fig-alt="The Quarto Preview terminal after a failed render: the counters 1/49 to 4/49 [count-emails], then Error: 'data_sumary' is not an exported object from 'namespace:datawizard', then Quitting from index.qmd:80-89 [count-emails], Execution halted and WARN: Error encountered when rendering files." width="100%" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: ::: {.column width="35%"} ::: {.small .fs-90} 1. **The error** repeats what R said: datawizard has no function `data_sumary` 2. **`Quitting from`** names the file, the lines of the chunk and its label 3. **The counter** `4/49 [count-emails]` shows how far knitr got 4. Correct the chunk, run it in the console, and render again ::: ::: :::: ::: notes A render can fail for many reasons, but in the first weeks most failures come from three places: a chunk that stops with an error, a header that is not valid YAML, and an object that exists in the console but is made by no chunk. Whatever the cause, the render stops, the Viewer keeps the last version that rendered, and the terminal says what went wrong. This one comes from a render in which the name of a function in the chunk that counts the emails was misspelt. Read it in three steps. The error line repeats what R itself said. The line beginning Quitting from names the file, the lines that hold the failing chunk and its label, which takes you straight to it. And the counter above the error shows how far knitr had got. The last two lines only confirm that the render stopped. ::: ## A render from a clean session {#a-render-from-a-clean-session .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="38%"} ::: {.small .fs-90} 1. Restart R (Ctrl+Shift+0), and watch the Variables pane empty 2. Open a new terminal with **+** in the Terminal tab, and type `quarto render` 3. Every chunk runs from the top, and the render ends with `Output created: _site\index.html` 4. Preview again, and check that every number is the one that you had before ::: ::: {.fragment .small .fs-90} A render that fails at a chunk which ran in the console has found an object that only the console had. Move the line that makes it into a chunk. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="62%"} ![](../tools/images/quarto/task-clean-render.png){fig-alt="A terminal in Positron at the end of the command quarto render in the folder replication-lab-housing-main, with the last lines reading Output created: _site\\index.html." width="100%" style="border: 1px solid #c9ced4; box-shadow: 1px 1px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);"} ::: :::: ::: notes The last step of every working session on a report is a render that starts from nothing, which shows whether the report makes everything that it uses. Quarto renders in a fresh R process of its own, whatever the state of your console, and the restart that comes first empties the console as well, so that the checks that you make afterwards start from the same blank state as the render. So restart R and watch the Variables pane empty. Then open a terminal and type quarto render: every chunk of the report runs from the top, and the render ends by naming the file that it wrote. Preview the report once more and check the numbers. [advance] If the render fails at a chunk that ran happily in the console, that chunk uses an object made by a line that you typed outside the chunks. Find the line and move it into the chunk where it belongs. ::: ## The project {#the-project .smaller .deepdive run="quarto"} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.fs-110} ```yaml project: type: website output-dir: _site render: - index.qmd execute: freeze: auto format: html: toc: true theme: cosmo code-fold: false code-tools: true ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.small} - `_quarto.yml` makes the folder a **project**, here without its comments and its title - `output-dir` sends the report to `_site`, and `render` limits the project to the report - `freeze: auto` runs a document again, in a render of the whole project, only when its source has changed, and keeps the results in `_freeze/` ::: ::: :::: ::: notes Put a file called underscore quarto dot yml beside a document and the folder becomes a project: a set of documents that share settings, render together and can be published as one thing. This is the configuration of the workspace, without its comments and its title. output dir sends the rendered site to the folder underscore site, which is why the report becomes underscore site slash index dot html, and render limits the project to the report, so that the Markdown codebooks in the data folder stay as they are. freeze auto tells Quarto, when it renders the whole project, to run a document again only when its source file has changed, and to keep the results in a folder called underscore freeze. A render of a single file always runs its code, whatever the setting says. The format block sets the defaults of every page at once. ::: ## From the folder to the record {#from-the-folder-to-the-record .smaller} ::: {.small} - **Render.** The rendered report carries the date of its run, from `date: today` in its header - **Version control.** The folder becomes a git repository, and every commit is a dated snapshot with a reason attached - **Publish.** Pushed to GitHub, the workspace renders the report and publishes it as a web page, through the workflow that it carries in `.github/` - **Archive.** A release deposited on Zenodo or the OSF gets a DOI and a version that does not change ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Today stops at the first step. The module Git and GitHub takes the next two on this same folder. ::: ::: notes Once the report renders, there are four steps between your folder and a public record, and today we take only the first. Rendering gives you a document that carries the date of its run. Version control turns the folder into a git repository, and every commit is then a dated snapshot of everything in it, with a sentence saying why it changed. Publishing pushes that repository to GitHub, and the workspace already carries a small workflow that renders the report there and publishes it as a web page every time that you push. And archiving deposits a release with Zenodo or the OSF, which gives it a DOI and a version that will not change, so that a paper can cite it, as the session on repositories set out this morning. [advance] The module Git and GitHub walks through the next two steps, click by click, on the folder that you have open now. ::: ## Hands-on 4 – A clean render {#hands-on-4-a-clean-render .smaller} ::: {.small} 1. Save the report with your edits of today 2. Restart R with Ctrl+Shift+0, or with the circular arrow at the top of the console 3. In a new terminal, type `quarto render` and wait for `Output created` 4. Preview the report with Ctrl+Shift+K, and check the counts, the figure, your computed sentence and your reference to Figure 1 ::: ::: {.fragment .small} RStudio: restart R, then **Render**. VS Code: restart the R terminal, then `quarto render` in a terminal of the folder. ::: ::: notes The last task of the day, and the one that I would most like you to make a habit. Save the report with all your edits of today, restart R, render the report from a terminal, and then preview it and check that everything is still there: the counts, the figure, the sentence whose number is now computed, and the reference to the figure. If the render fails, read the message from the top, as we did a few slides ago, and fix the chunk that it names. A report that renders from a clean session is a report that someone else can render on their own machine and get the same numbers, which is the first of the three Rs of this morning. [advance] In RStudio and VS Code the steps have the same shape. Take the time you need. ::: ## The next session and the reading {#next-session} ::: {.small .nonincremental} - **The next session** opens the second day, the one-day workshop on the case of your course, in four parts: the claim and credibility, the estimand and the causal graph, the reproduction, and robustness. Its work is done in the report of the workspace of your case, a Quarto document of the kind taken apart today - **The reading of this session** is the module Quarto documents, which knits small documents in your browser and ends with six tasks in the workspace. The module Git and GitHub then takes the folder of the report into version control ::: ::: {.urlbox} [[codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/quarto.html](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/quarto.html)]{.fs-80} ::: ::: {.urlbox} [[codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/git-github.html](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/git-github.html)]{.fs-80} ::: ::: notes That closes the first day. This afternoon you used R on one file, found your way round the IDE, and took apart the report that the rest of the course is written in, ending with a render from a clean session. The reading of this session is the module Quarto documents, whose first sections knit small documents in your browser and whose section of tasks, near the end, holds the six that you did today in the workspace, so that you can repeat them at home. The module Git and GitHub takes the same folder into version control, which is the next step in the life of a report. <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
